clue.text: One out of the middle of the bat for epic poet

definitions.text: One out of the middle of the bat
definitions.meaning: in baseball a home run, struck clean off the sweet spot of the bat, is called by this slang name
the blind Greek bard credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey

explanation.surface: A ball hit sweetly off the bat is somehow tied to an ancient poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek author of the Iliad and Odyssey is the archetypal composer of epic verse.

clue.text: 27 of history

parts.note: 27 across supplies the words 'the father', so the clue reads as the traditional title of the Greek historian Cicero hailed as founder of history writing

explanation.surface: A cross-reference asks for a famous title given to an ancient writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Cicero called this Greek writer of the Persian Wars 'the Father of History'; the clue borrows THE FATHER from 27 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero's honorific for the Greek chronicler of the Persian Wars was pater historiae, father of history.

clue.text: State of Eberhart's verse

parts.note: the American poet Richard Eberhart summered on the coast of this New England state and wrote many poems set there

explanation.surface: A question about where an American poet set his poems.
explanation.definitionFit: The New England state on the Atlantic coast where Richard Eberhart spent summers is the setting of much of his poetry.

clue.text: Buckler chronicled this rising of the young David

definitions.text: Buckler chronicled this rising of the young David

parts.words: Buckler chronicled this rising of the young David
parts.note: a writer named Buckler told the story of an uprising led by the young David, and the clue asks for the word for such a rising

explanation.surface: A historian is said to have recorded a young man's uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising is an armed revolt against authority, which is what an insurrection or uprising means.

clue.text: Flute played at her nuptials

parts.note: Francis Flute the bellows-mender acts Thisbe in the mechanicals' play staged for the wedding of Theseus and the Amazon queen in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: It sounds as if a woodwind instrument was heard at someone's wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flute' looks like the instrument but is the Shakespearean character who performs at the royal wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: In A Midsummer Night's Dream the Amazon queen weds Theseus, and Flute plays Thisbe at the celebration.

clue.text: Rogue exposed by Walpole

parts.note: Hugh Walpole's 1930 novel Rogue ... is named after its Cumbrian hero, Francis, a wild member of a landed family

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is unmasked by an eighteenth-century prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Walpole looks like Robert Walpole the politician; it is Hugh Walpole the novelist, and 'Rogue' is the first word of his novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname completes the title of Hugh Walpole's novel about the rogue Francis of that family.

clue.text: New staples for drawing

definitions.note: the phrase describes things used for drawing, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters of the following word are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A fresh supply of paper fasteners is needed for the art class.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft coloured crayons are sticks used to make drawings.

explanation.definitionFit: This is an old name for a thrush; White wrote of the ring variety visiting Hampshire in autumn.

clue.text: Bell memorialized some of its eminences

definitions.text: Bell memorialized some of its eminences

parts.words: Bell memorialized some of its eminences
parts.note: a writer named Bell commemorated notable figures, or heights, of a northern English county

explanation.surface: A biographer wrote tributes to the great figures of a region.

clue.text: Musketeer in Macedonia

explanation.surface: A French soldier finds himself in the Balkans.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumas's musketeer and the monastic peninsula mountain in Macedonia carry the same name.

clue.text: Picture of fliers from New Zealand. Frame provided

explanation.definitionFit: Janet Frame's novel The ... takes its title from birds whose call is thought to foretell wet weather.

clue.text: Possibly a rash friend of naval officer

clue.text: People like Kant and Berkeley who have notions about a leaning

a leaning or tilt, as of a ship, is a list

explanation.surface: Philosophers who hold opinions about a slant.
explanation.definitionFit: Kant and Berkeley held that reality depends on mind, the doctrine of philosophical idealism.

clue.text: Offstage alarms are venomous, they say

explanation.surface: Warnings off stage are said to be poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: Stage directions in old plays often call for alarm bells sounded offstage.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarm bells rung as warnings, often called for in stage directions.

clue.text: Old king figures in my celeb characters

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch appears in a gossip column about my famous friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' rearranges IN MY CELEB; 'figures' is a link meaning appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A legendary early king of Britain, the title figure of a Shakespeare play.

clue.text: Favour for Canadian poet

Robert W. ..., the bard of the Yukon gold rush

explanation.surface: Asking a good turn of a Canadian poet.
explanation.definitionFit: A favour is a kindness rendered; Robert Service wrote The Shooting of Dan McGrew.

clue.text: Verse tool ingeniously used by president

explanation.surface: A head of state cleverly employs poetry as a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Two American heads of state, Theodore and Franklin, bore this surname.

clue.text: Benchley's birdcatcher?

explanation.surface: A humorist's idea of what catches birds.

explanation.definitionFit: Inverting the proverb, the worm that rises early gets caught by the bird.

clue.text: Some inn could reveal crime writer

clue.text: One of Ballantyne's trail-blazers, or one of Cooper's?

clue.text: "That transatlantic dram which is poetically named an —" (Dickens, Our Mutual Friend)

clue.text: Extremes of energy retain record panegyric

explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremes of' takes E and Y from 'energy'; 'retain' puts LOG between them.

clue.text: … indicating two quartets?

explanation.definitionFit: A group of eight performers, as two sets of four make together.
